newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian inflation stable but food, services rise.
newsitem.headline: Croatian inflation stable but food, services rise.

text.p: A steady increase in some food and services prices in Croatia must be watched even though monthly inflation remained stable in April, continuing this year's trend, an independent analyst said on Tuesday.
Official figures released on Tuesday showed April retail prices rose 0.1 percent month on month and 4.4 percent from last year.
"The inflation is generally low and constant, without any quickening or slowing of the trend," Zarko Miljenovic, chief economist at leading Zagrebacka Banka, told Reuters.
Although monthly prices have shown very little change over the last few months, prices rose more compared to last year than they have since August when they gained 4.7 percent.
Miljenovic warned the government must apply restraint in its measures designed to aid farmers, in order to prevent the entire food sector getting out of hand.
Various agricultural and seasonal produce jumped 0.3-0.9 percent from March and up to five percent compared to April 1996, rising faster than most other goods.
"Import quotas and guaranteed prices of some agricultural produce might eventually translate into higher food prices," Miljenovic said.

Services recorded an 8.7 percent annual increase which Miljenovic put down to a lack of competition in the sector. However they only gained 0.1 percent on March, in line with the general monthly rise.

Miljenovic pointed to utilities prices as a typical example because of the state monopoly system, and also personal services such as hairdressing. "This rise is not new. It has been carried over from January, when transport fees and postal services (prices) went up."
In addition to poor competition the service sector has also been affected by stronger personal demand, boosted by sizeable wage increases over the past two years.
"Unlike in the real sector, these pressures are slowly built into the services prices," Miljenovic said.
The government set the 1997 inflation target within a three to five percent range, but January-April retail prices were 4.1 percent higher than in the same period last year.

"But there is no cause for alarm yet, although all this should be watched to avoid a new vicious circle being started," he added, referring to the spiralling inflation Croatia experienced some years ago.
Producer prices were unchanged in April but showed a 1.9 percent rise on last year.
